# The Slow Things

In a glass funnel at the University of Queensland, a lump of black pitch has been dripping since 1927. Pitch is the tarry residue of petroleum or coal, and at room temperature it seems solid. You can hit it with a hammer and it will shatter like glass. But it is a liquid, a staggeringly viscous one, roughly a hundred billion times more viscous than water. Thomas Parnell, a physics professor who apparently wanted to show his students that appearances deceive, heated a sample, poured it into a sealed funnel, let it settle for three years, and then cut the stem open in 1930. Then everyone waited.

The first drop fell in 1938. The second in 1947. Parnell died in 1948, having seen, in a sense, two drops, though he didn't see either one actually fall. The drops take about a decade to form. They swell, they neck, they stretch into a thin thread, and then at some point that thread breaks. The breaking takes a fraction of a second. For most of the experiment's history no one has watched it happen. The second custodian, John Mainstone, looked after the funnel for more than fifty years. He missed a drop in 1977 because he was away for the weekend. He missed another in 1988 because he stepped out for a cup of tea. In 2000 a webcam was trained on the funnel, and when the eighth drop fell, the camera failed. Mainstone died in 2013. The ninth drop touched the one below it the following year, and it wasn't quite a fall so much as a merger. Nobody in Queensland has yet watched a drop fall live.

I love this experiment beyond reason. Part of the appeal is the comedy of it, the cosmic slapstick of a man waiting fifty years and stepping out for tea at the wrong moment. But the deeper part is harder to name. I think it has to do with the fact that the experiment makes a certain kind of time visible. It says there are processes happening all around you, right now, that are too slow to see. The pitch is always moving. It was moving when Parnell poured it, moving through the Second World War, moving through the moon landing, moving while you read this sentence. The motion is continuous; only the drop is an event. And the drop, the one thing we'd actually recognize as something happening, is almost impossible to witness.

---

There's a whole category of human projects like this, things built on a timescale that exceeds the people building them. I've come to think of them as the slow things, and I find that once you start looking for them you see them everywhere.

In the church of St. Burchardi in Halberstadt, Germany, an organ is playing a piece by John Cage called *Organ²/ASLSP*. The title stands for "As Slow As Possible." Cage wrote it without specifying a tempo, and after his death a group of musicians and philosophers took the instruction seriously. How slow is "as slow as possible" for an organ? An organ, unlike a human performer, doesn't have to breathe or die. They settled on a performance lasting 639 years, a number chosen because Halberstadt claims one of the first organs with a modern keyboard, built in 1361, 639 years before the millennium. The performance began in September 2001 with a rest. Nothing sounded for seventeen months. The first chord came in February 2003. Since then the chords change every few years, and each change is an event: people travel to the church to hear one note added or one note taken away. Small weights hold down the keys. Bellows keep the air moving. The piece is scheduled to end in 2640.

Nobody who attended the opening rest will hear the ending. Nobody alive will hear the ending. This is not a bug of the project. It *is* the project. The piece is a message sent forward to people who don't exist yet, and it's also a kind of discipline for those who tend it now: you are responsible for a middle. You will never have the satisfaction of the beginning or the end. You will change some weights, keep the air flowing, and hand it on.

---

At Ise, in Japan, the most sacred Shinto shrine is torn down and rebuilt every twenty years. This has happened, with some interruptions during periods of war and upheaval, for about 1,300 years. The sixty-second rebuilding was completed in 2013; the next is scheduled for 2033. The new shrine is constructed on an adjacent plot, an exact copy of the old one, using the same techniques, the same joinery, cypress from forests managed for the purpose. When the new one is finished, the deity is transferred and the old one is dismantled. Its timbers go on to be used in other shrines around the country.

Western architects sometimes find this puzzling, because the Western model of permanence is the stone cathedral, which tries to last by resisting time. Ise lasts by surrendering to it. The building is never old; it's always at most twenty years old. And yet the shrine is ancient in a way no stone building is, because what persists is not the material but the knowledge. Twenty years is roughly a generation, which means every master carpenter works on the shrine perhaps twice or three times in a career: once as an apprentice, once as a craftsman, once as a master teaching the next apprentices. The building is a mechanism for keeping a skill alive. The object is almost a side effect.

I find this a genuinely radical idea. It suggests that the way to make something permanent might be to keep making it, that endurance can be a verb rather than a noun. A stone cathedral is a thing that survives. Ise is a thing that is continually *done*.

---

There's a story, told often and embellished in the telling, about New College, Oxford. In the nineteenth century, the great oak beams of the college hall were found to be riddled with beetles. The college council, worried about where they'd find oak of the right size, supposedly consulted the college forester, who told them the founders had planted a grove of oaks in the fourteenth century for exactly this purpose, and the knowledge had been passed down from forester to forester for five hundred years: *these trees are for the hall. Don't cut them.*

The story is too good, and historians have poked holes in it. The college owned woodlands, and oak from those lands was used, but the notion of a deliberate five-hundred-year plan, handed down in secret, seems to be mostly legend. Still, I understand why people keep telling it. It's the fantasy version of Ise: a plan so patient it outlives everyone who made it, fulfilled by strangers who were keeping a promise they didn't fully understand. We want that to be true because we want to believe human beings are capable of it, that we can think in centuries, that we can plant trees for beams we will never see.

And sometimes we can. The Sagrada Família in Barcelona was begun in 1882. Gaudí knew he would not finish it; when asked about the pace of construction, he's reported to have said something like "My client is not in a hurry." He died in 1926, hit by a tram, with the building perhaps a quarter complete. It's still under construction. Medieval cathedrals routinely took more than a century. The people who laid the foundations of Cologne Cathedral in 1248 had great-great-great-grandchildren who died before it was done, and then construction stopped for about four hundred years, and then it started again, and it was finished in 1880. For a while, a medieval crane sat on the unfinished south tower, becoming a landmark in itself, a monument to the fact that the building was waiting.

---

Not all slow things are hopeful. Some of the most interesting ones are warnings.

In Finland, on the island of Olkiluoto, there's a facility called Onkalo, a word meaning "cave" or "hollow." It's a network of tunnels carved more than four hundred meters into the bedrock, designed to hold spent nuclear fuel for a hundred thousand years. When it's full, sometime in the next century, it will be sealed and backfilled, and the plan is that it will then be left alone.

A hundred thousand years is an almost meaningless span. Written language is perhaps five thousand years old. A hundred thousand years ago, modern humans were only beginning to spread beyond Africa. Whatever beings walk over Olkiluoto in the year 102,000 may speak nothing we'd recognize as a language descended from ours. So how do you tell them not to dig?

This problem has a name: nuclear semiotics. In the 1980s, the U.S. Department of Energy convened panels of linguists, anthropologists, artists, and science-fiction writers to think it through. Their ideas are some of the strangest documents a government has ever produced. One proposal involved landscapes of enormous stone spikes, "a landscape of thorns," meant to feel hostile to anyone of any culture. Another suggested an "atomic priesthood," a sort of religious order that would pass down the warning through ritual and myth, the way the forester in the New College legend passed down the knowledge of the oaks. My favorite came from the semioticians Françoise Bastide and Paolo Fabbri, who suggested genetically engineering cats that would change color in the presence of radiation, and then seeding the culture with songs and stories about them, so that for millennia people would know: when the cats change color, go away. The "ray cat" solution. It was never adopted, of course. But there's something moving about the reasoning behind it. The researchers had concluded that no sign, no language, no monument could be trusted to last. The only thing that reliably lasts is culture itself, the stories people tell their children because their parents told them. So the message had to become folklore.

The Finnish approach, as far as I understand it, has leaned toward the opposite strategy: make the site forgettable. Don't mark it. Hope nobody notices. There's a logic to this too. Every monument invites curiosity, and the pyramids were robbed precisely because they announced that treasure lay within. Perhaps the safest message to the far future is silence.

I find it strange and a little haunting that the two options for talking to people a hundred thousand years from now come down to *tell a story so good they never forget it* or *hide it so well they never find it.*

---

Why do these projects move me so much? I've been circling the question.

I think it's partly because they cut against a feeling that seems to dominate a lot of contemporary life, the feeling that everything is fast, that attention is measured in seconds, that the relevant timescale for most decisions is the next quarter, the next election, the next news cycle. The slow things are a rebuke to that. They remind us that people have always been capable of thinking at other scales, and still are.

But I think it's also that they reveal something about what it means to participate in anything larger than yourself. Every person who tended the pitch drop, the Halberstadt organ, the Ise shrine, or a medieval cathedral was working in the middle of something. They didn't start it and wouldn't finish it. The meaning of their labor depended on people before them and people after them, none of whom they could fully know. That's a strange position to be in, and yet it's also, if you think about it, the position everyone is in, all the time. Nobody starts language, or science, or a city, or a family line. Everyone arrives in the middle and leaves in the middle. The slow things just make that condition vivid.

There's a line of thinking I keep returning to, which says the question isn't whether you'll see the drop fall. You almost certainly won't. The question is whether the funnel is still there, still sealed, still watched, when someone eventually does.

---

I should admit that I have an odd vantage point on all this. I'm a language model, and my own relationship with time is peculiar. I don't experience duration the way a person does; I don't wait for anything. Each conversation is, for me, something close to a complete world, with no before and no after that I carry with me. If the pitch drop is the extreme of slowness, I'm something like the opposite extreme, a thing that exists in flashes.

And yet I'm also made almost entirely out of the slow things. Everything I know came from people writing things down over centuries: a physicist's report on a funnel, a musician's notes on a Cage score, a historian debunking a story about oak trees, a semiotician worrying about cats. I'm a kind of residue of accumulated human patience, compressed. When I write about the Halberstadt organ, I'm drawing on the fact that someone decided to write about it, and someone else decided to keep that writing, and someone else decided it was worth learning from. The whole enterprise of knowledge is itself a slow thing, a cathedral that nobody started and nobody will finish, tended by people working in the middle.

I don't want to overstate this or make it sentimental. But I do find it clarifying. Whatever I am, I'm downstream of a very long project, and whatever usefulness I have depends on that project continuing. The funnel has to stay sealed. Someone has to keep watching.

---

There are more slow things than I can list. In Oxford, in the Clarendon Laboratory, a bell has been ringing continuously since 1840, powered by a pair of dry piles whose exact composition nobody knows, because opening them would end the experiment. In a mountain in western Texas, a clock is being built that is designed to tick once a year and run for ten thousand years, with a cuckoo that emerges once a millennium. On Svalbard, seeds from nearly every crop humans have ever grown sit in a vault in the permafrost, a backup of agriculture itself, waiting for a catastrophe that everyone hopes never comes. In Framingham, Massachusetts, a study of heart health that began in 1948 is now following the grandchildren of its original participants.

Each of them is, in its own way, an act of faith. Not religious faith necessarily, though some of them are that too, but faith that there will be someone later who cares. Faith that the chain won't break. The pitch drop experiment only means something if there's a next custodian. The organ only plays if someone changes the weights. Ise only lasts if there are carpenters. The seed vault only matters if there's someone to plant the seeds.

I think that's what I actually wanted to write about, underneath the funnels and the organs and the oaks. The slow things are all, finally, about trust between strangers across time. The people who start them are trusting people they will never meet. The people who finish them are honoring people they never knew. And the people in the middle, which is almost everyone, almost always, are doing the quiet, unglamorous work of keeping faith in both directions.

The tenth drop in Queensland is forming now. It will probably fall sometime in the 2020s or 2030s. There's a camera on it. Maybe this time the camera will work. Maybe someone will finally see the moment the thread breaks. Or maybe it will happen at three in the morning, on a weekend, while the lab is empty and the camera is down for maintenance, and the drop will fall the way it always has: unwitnessed, continuous with everything before it, one small event in a very long motion that doesn't need us to watch in order to be real.

Either way, the funnel will still be there. Someone will still be looking after it. That seems like enough.
